tier_justification: Re-derivation of Rice's theorem (Rice 1953) by the standard recursion-theorem argument with a swapped case split (as in Yanofsky 2003, the Coq development coq-synthetic-computability, and Mathlib's ComputablePred.rice), restated over an abstract system in which the recursion theorem is an assumption.
plain_claim: In any programming system satisfying the fixpoint principle (every admissible transformer f has a code c with sem (f c) = sem c), no nontrivial extensional predicate P on codes is decided inside the system: there is no checker that decides P and all of whose switches c ↦ if chk c then a else b are admissible.
notes: No global closure law on Adm is assumed as a separate hypothesis; the only admissibility the proof uses is that of one switch on the checker, which is part of DecidedInside (see R2). The class form, for any class K of checkers all of whose switches are admissible (K ⊆ SwitchAdmissible S), is the corollary Toy.Rice.not_decidedBy_of_fixpointPrinciple_switchClosed_extensional_nontrivial.

depth_note: Apply the fixpoint principle to the swapped switch and case on the checker's verdict at the fixed point.
nonvacuity_witness: The padded system with BehTrue and the flat domain with Halts satisfy all hypotheses.
lawvere_relation: Lawvere's theorem: if every map in a class is represented by a point, every endomorphism whose diagonal lies in the class has a fixed point. Here the fixpoint principle plays the role of that conclusion, and the swapped switch on a decider of a nontrivial extensional P moves every code to a code of the other P-status, acting on the two P-classes like Boolean negation, which has no fixed point. F3 shows the fixpoint principle itself is a Lawvere-style diagonal consequence of representability.
non_claims: Does not forbid: (i) partial or one-sided procedures: a one-sided switch that answers on the codes satisfying the predicate and diverges on the others can be admissible while the predicate is not decided inside (W8, Toy.Rice.Flat.halts_unswappedSwitch_admissible_not_decidedInside, in the flat-domain system); semi-decision itself is not formalized; (ii) checkers for decidable fragments: a separate total language without the fixpoint principle decides a nontrivial extensional predicate inside (N1), and a behaviour-closed fragment of a system whose transformers cannot test code equality does as well (W4); R6 states when restricting to a behaviour-closed fragment does not help; (iii) sound but incomplete checkers: these are switch-admissible in systems with the fixpoint principle (W1, W2), and W5 states the incompleteness every such checker of a nontrivial extensional predicate has.

'Not decided inside the system' is not 'no Boolean function decides P'. Decides is a set-theoretic relation that classical logic always satisfies; the impossibility concerns the admissibility of the switches on such a function. For example Toy.Rice.Flat.haltCheck decides halting on the flat domain but is not switch-admissible (Toy.Rice.Examples.switchAdmissible_neg).

The strength of the conclusion depends entirely on how rich Adm is. The fixpoint principle becomes easier to satisfy as Adm shrinks; with no admissible transformers it holds vacuously and then nothing at all is decided inside (Toy.Rice.Controls.emptyAdm_fixpointPrinciple_nothingDecided). The result rules out only checkers whose switches are admissible.
The converse fails: a system without the fixpoint principle need not decide anything nontrivial, even if it contains all constants and is closed under composition (N3).
Says nothing about semi-decision: DecidedInside is two-sided, and a one-sided switch can be admissible while the two-sided decision is impossible (W8). The Rice-Shapiro theorem is not formalized.

Says nothing about time or space: Adm is a bare membership predicate with no cost model. It neither shows nor refutes complexity-aware versions (for example Asperti 2008, listed under Prior art), which are not covered.

Applies only to extensional predicates, relative to the chosen semantics sem. Properties of code text can be decided inside a system with the fixpoint principle (W3). Which predicates count as extensional depends on sem.

Does not forbid certificate checking (proof-carrying or annotation-assisted verification): deciding 'the attached certificate is valid' for a code that carries a certificate is a property of the text, not of the behaviour alone, and such checks can be switch-admissible in a system with the fixpoint principle (compare W2). Such a checker is sound for P but complete only for codes carrying a valid certificate, not for P itself.

Decides and DecidedInside quantify deterministically over every code. Says nothing about randomized checkers, classifiers that are accurate on a distribution or benchmark, or checkers verified only on bounded inputs.
Says nothing about any particular real language unless that language's fixpoint principle is established; the connection to acceptable numberings is a modeling bridge, not a theorem here.

tier_justification: Abstract form of the classical recursive-inseparability obstruction (Kleene 1950): with code-equality tests available, restricting to a behaviour-closed fragment such as the halting programs does not make a nontrivial extensional property decided inside the restricted system. plain_claim: Let S have the fixpoint principle, let its admissible transformers be closed under literal code-equality tests (for admissible f and codes k, a, b, the transformer c ↦ if f c = k then a else b is admissible), and let F be a fragment of codes closed under same behaviour. hypotheses.purpose: Forces the fixed point, which behaves like a fragment code, into the fragment.

tier_justification: Abstract form of Kleene's (second) recursion theorem via a diagonal (as in Yanofsky 2003 and Lemma FP of coq-synthetic-computability), with the closure hypothesis weakened to closure under precomposition with the diagonal.
plain_claim: If every admissible transformer is computed by some code under a partial application app (Represents), d is a diagonal transformer (whenever app x x halts with output z, the code d x behaves like z), and precomposition with d preserves admissibility, then for every admissible f some code e computes f ∘ d, and for every such e the code d e is a semantic fixed point of f (sem (f (d e)) = sem (d e)). In particular the system has the fixpoint principle.

hypotheses.purpose: d e behaves like the output of e on itself.

hypotheses.purpose: f ∘ d is admissible, so hrep applies to it.

depth_note: Instantiate hrep at f ∘ d and hdiag at e; the same two-step pattern as F1.

non_claims: Does not forbid any checker design by itself: it derives the fixpoint principle from representability. What follows for checkers follows through R1, R2, R4, R6 and W5 to W7, and partial or one-sided procedures (W8), checkers for decidable fragments (N1, W4), and sound but incomplete checkers (W1, W2) remain possible under those results.

Does not construct an acceptable numbering; Represents, IsDiagonal and PrecompClosed are assumptions. Establishing them for a real language needs a universal function and the s-m-n theorem (a modeling bridge).

The fixpoint principle does not require Turing-completeness, universal programs, or self-reference: the flat-domain, padded and lifted systems satisfy it without encoding computation (and without this theorem's hypotheses).

PrecompClosed S d is strictly weaker than the textbook pair CompClosed S and Adm d: in the tag model PrecompClosed holds while Adm d fails. The textbook corollary is kept as Toy.Rice.fixpointPrinciple_of_compClosed_represents_diagonal.

tier_justification: Folklore (Rice-style arguments need the recursion theorem; weak total formalisms escape them) made precise in a concrete toy system.
plain_claim: In the lookup-table system (codes: finite tables; behaviours: total functions ℕ → ℕ; admissible transformers: those expressible in the total language TProg of constant tables, identity, two table edits, composition, and conditionals on the tests of a small test language TTest), the fixpoint principle fails and the nontrivial extensional predicate 'computes the zero function' is decided inside the system by zeroCheck, which is itself a TTest test.
notes: Existence statement about one concrete system: Tables.sys witnesses that a system can lack the fixpoint principle and decide a nontrivial extensional predicate inside. Nothing follows for other total languages (see the non-claims).
depth_note: The fixpoint failure is immediate (incrAt 0 changes the value at 0); correctness of zeroCheck is a short induction. Toy.Rice.Tables.tail_not_admissible shows the admissible class is proper. Further checkers and predicates are covered by Toy.Rice.Tables.allOutputsZero_switchAdmissible (every switch on the syntactic checker allOutputsZero t = t.all (fun p => p.2 == 0), 'every stored value is 0', is admissible), Toy.Rice.Tables.evalAtZero_decidedInside (the pointwise predicate 'the value at 0 is 0' is decided inside) and Toy.Rice.Tables.isNil_decidedInside (the syntactic predicate 'the table is empty' is decided inside).
nonvacuity_witness: The statement is closed and concrete.
model_notes: Codes: List (ℕ × ℕ), first entry wins, default 0. Behaviours: ℕ → ℕ. Adm f := ∃ p : TProg, ∀ x, p.run x = f x. zeroCheck t = TTest.run t (TTest.allEntries (EntryTest.evalAtKeyEq 0)), by rfl (Toy.Rice.Tables.zeroCheck_eq_test).
non_claims: Is itself an example of what Rice-style results do not forbid: an internal decider for a nontrivial extensional predicate in a total language without the fixpoint principle. It does not show that such a decider exists for an expressive total language (see the primitive-recursive modeling bridge), and it says nothing for or against partial or semi-decision procedures or sound but incomplete checkers, which are not needed here because the predicate is decided.

'Computes the zero function' is decided inside this system because a finite table has finite support, so 'zero everywhere' reduces to finitely many evaluations. This is not a property of total languages in general: for primitive-recursive programs (equivalently Loop programs, Meyer and Ritchie 1967, Theorem 7), 'computes the zero function' is not decidable by any total computable procedure (classical undecidability; see the modeling bridge, which is not formalized).

Pointwise behavioural properties, such as 'the value at 0 is 0' (Toy.Rice.Tables.evalAtZero_decidedInside), can be decided by evaluating the program at finitely many inputs in any total language whose programs can be run (decidability in the classical computability sense; commentary, not formalized beyond this system); universally quantified properties such as 'computes the zero function' or program equivalence are a different matter (previous item).
Does not claim that every total language decides every extensional property, nor that totality is the only way to lose the fixpoint principle.

TProg and TTest are a deliberately small language over a deliberately weak code type; the system shows that deciding this predicate inside is consistent once the fixpoint principle is dropped, not that a comparable checker exists for an expressive language.

modeling_bridges.label: derived (modeling bridge)
modeling_bridges.claim: For primitive-recursive programs, 'computes the zero function' is not decidable in the classical sense: no total computable procedure decides it on program indices.
modeling_bridges.reasoning: By Kleene's normal form theorem the predicate T(e, x, s) ('machine e on input x halts within s steps') is primitive recursive, so f_e(s) = 1 if T(e, e, s) else 0 is primitive recursive, uniformly in e, and f_e is the zero function iff machine e does not halt on input e. A decider for 'computes the zero function' on primitive-recursive programs would therefore decide the complement of the halting problem (standard; see Kleene 1952 and Rogers 1967). Not formalized here.

tier_justification: A concrete instance of R1 in a three-point flat domain; the fixpoint principle there is the least-fixed-point argument behind Kleene's first recursion theorem.
plain_claim: In the flat-domain system (codes and behaviours are the three denotations 'diverges', 'returns true', 'returns false'; sem is the identity; admissible transformers are the monotone maps), the fixpoint principle holds, halting is extensional and nontrivial, and halting is not decided inside the system.
notes: Existence statement about one concrete system: Flat.sys witnesses that the fixpoint principle, a nontrivial extensional predicate, and the failure to decide it inside occur together. It is not a statement about other systems.
depth_note: Every monotone map on the three-point flat domain has a fixed point (iterate from bot); then R1.
non_claims: Does not forbid: (i) partial or one-sided procedures: in this same system the one-sided switch 'if the program halts then return true, else diverge' is admissible (W8); semi-decision itself is not formalized; (ii) checkers for decidable fragments: the two-element total fragment of this system decides every predicate (Toy.Rice.Flat.totalSys_decides_every_predicate), a degenerate case recorded as Toy.Rice.Examples.restrict_degenerate_flat; (iii) sound but incomplete checkers: the statement concerns deciders only; because the only switch-admissible checkers here are constant (Toy.Rice.Flat.switchAdmissible_const), a sound switch-admissible checker for halting can only be the one that rejects everything.

'Halting is not decided inside' is not 'no Boolean function decides halting': haltCheck decides Halts on the flat domain (Toy.Rice.Flat.haltCheck_decides); what fails is the admissibility of its swapped switch (Toy.Rice.Examples.switchAdmissible_neg). No classical undecidability of halting is claimed or formalized here; the classical fact is cited in prose only (W8).
Codes are denotations (sem = id), so every predicate is extensional; this system cannot separate syntactic from semantic predicates (see the padded system, W2 and W3).

Only the two constant checkers are switch-admissible here (Toy.Rice.Flat.switchAdmissible_const), so every nontrivial predicate fails to be decided inside for a blunt reason. The system is a positive control for R1's hypotheses, not a model of a programming language.

The fixpoint principle holds here by a least-fixed-point argument on a pointed poset, with no encoding of computation, universal program, or self-reference: the fixpoint principle does not imply Turing-completeness.
The flat domain is not a lattice (Toy.Rice.Flat.no_upper_bound_tt_ff), so this is not an instance of Tarski's lattice fixed-point theorem.

model_notes: Codes: Option Table (none = the divergent program). Behaviours: Option (ℕ → ℕ), sem = Option.map eval. non_claims: Is itself a checker for a decidable fragment, which Rice-style results do not forbid when the system's transformers cannot test code equality (compare R6). It says nothing about partial or semi-decision procedures (not formalized; compare W8) or about sound but incomplete checkers on the full system beyond the degeneracy that only constant checkers are switch-admissible there (Toy.Rice.Lifted.switchAdmissible_const).

The escape relies on strictness: the full-system transformer that agrees with a fragment switch sends the divergent code to the divergent code, which models an analyzer allowed to diverge outside the fragment. Under closure under code-equality tests the escape is impossible for every behaviour-closed fragment (R6). In particular, for a Turing-complete language with total computable code transformers, restricting to the halting programs does not make 'returns true' decidable in the classical sense, by a total computable procedure on the halting programs (modeling bridge of R6, not formalized; Kleene 1950).

In the full system Toy.Rice.Lifted.sys only the two constant checkers are switch-admissible (Toy.Rice.Lifted.switchAdmissible_const): a switch whose two branches are halting codes does not send the divergent code to itself, so it is admissible only if it is constant. Hence every nontrivial predicate on the full system, syntactic ones included, fails to be decided inside it (Toy.Rice.Lifted.not_decidedInside_of_nontrivial; for example 'the code is the empty table', Toy.Rice.Lifted.isEmptyTable_not_decidedInside), for the same strictness reason as in the flat-domain system (N2, Toy.Rice.Flat.switchAdmissible_const). The full-system conjunct ¬ DecidedInside sys HaltsZero therefore carries no information beyond this degeneracy. The content of W4 lies in the halting fragment Lifted.totalSys, whose admissible class is proper (it excludes the tail map) and contains the non-constant switch-admissible checker fragCheck.
Deciding on the fragment does not give a decider on the full system: membership in the fragment (halting) is extensional and nontrivial in the full system, hence not decided inside it (R1).

The full system's fixpoint principle holds for a domain-theoretic reason (every admissible transformer is constant or fixes the divergent code); the system is not Turing-complete and not a model of a real language.

The two-element total fragment of the flat-domain system admits every map and decides every predicate (Toy.Rice.Examples.restrict_degenerate_flat); it is recorded as a degenerate example and not used as evidence.

plain_claim: In a system with the fixpoint principle, let chk be switch-admissible and sound for an extensional predicate P that some code violates. Then every realizable behaviour (the behaviour of some code) has a code that chk rejects: for every code a there is a code c with sem c = sem a and chk c = false. In particular every code satisfying P, and every accepted code, has a rejected code with the same behaviour.
